title: Where to Wear? A talk on frictional wear

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Every surface has a biography written by frictional contact. That's the opening line of a talk Antoine gave in Toronto, and it makes you look at a worn bathroom tile differently.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: A bathroom tile has a biography? Okay, you have my attention. What was the talk?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It was called Where to Wear? Antoine presented it with Sheldon Andrews from ÉTS at GraphQuon 2025, the Quebec and Ontario pre-SIGGRAPH workshop, held on November 15 and 16 at the University of Toronto. The big idea is that time, contact and energy loss change how a surface looks and behaves.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So wear, like scratches on a tool?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. Worn patterns on tile in an engineering school, scratches on tools, gaming materials, even robot grippers. The talk shows how to predict that wear and turn it into something graphics can use.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: How does it get from physics to pictures?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It starts with the mechanics, Archard wear and energy-based wear laws. Then comes a graphics pipeline. You build a contact mask, use orthographic volumes, work out tangential velocity and traction, and integrate all that into the texture. Think of a path through a lawn: the more feet walk there, the more the grass wears, and the texture records the story.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And how do you check that it looks right?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The deck covers validation ideas too, like capturing real surfaces with a GelSight sensor and interpolating from a materials atlas.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's where graphics labs from Quebec and Ontario share work before SIGGRAPH season: short talks, posters, honest feedback from people who build simulators and renderers. Antoine had helped build the GraphQuon 2024 site at ÉTS, so presenting in Toronto felt like the same community, just a few hours down the road.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Is this connected to his other work?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, it connects to his research at ÉTS on three-D fabrication and validation of frictional surfaces.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And what did he take away from it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That a talk can surface good questions before a paper exists, and that the hallway conversations mattered as much as the podium.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Nice. The write-up has the pipeline diagram, the full slide deck to download, and a few photos from Toronto.
